extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: A dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions crowdsourced using a novel method that leverages a large corpus of domain-specific text and existing questions to aid question generation.
extraction.license: Creative Commons Attribution-Non-Commercial 3.0 Unported (CC BY-NC 3.0) License
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions, Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner, arXiv:1707.06209v1 [cs.HC] 19 Jul 2017
extraction.rai:dataCollection: A two-step crowdsourcing process was used: (1) crowd workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs and asked to select one and formulate a question-answer pair about it, and (2) another worker validated the question and generated three answer distractors aided by model suggestions. The method leveraged a corpus of 28 science study textbooks from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Science study textbooks from various online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science and physics spanning elementary level to college introductory material. A total of 28 books were compiled and used as the base corpus.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A rule-based document filter was applied to individual paragraphs of the base corpus. The filter classified individual sentences and accepted a paragraph if a minimum number of sentences was accepted. Filter rules included lexical, grammatical, pragmatical and complexity based criteria such as: filtering out questions/exclamations, sentences without verb phrases, those with modal verbs, imperative phrases, demonstrative pronouns, personal pronouns other than third-person, sentences beginning with pronouns, containing first names, having less than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas, containing special characters other than punctuation, having more than three tokens beginning uppercase, mentioning graphs/tables/web links, beginning with discourse markers, containing absolute wording, or containing instructional vocabulary.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two-step annotation process: (1) Question Formulation Task: Workers were presented with three filtered textbook paragraphs, chose one, and formulated a question-answer pair. Instructions specified desirable characteristics: no yes/no questions, not requiring further context, querying general principles rather than highly specific facts, question length between 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguous questions, answers clear from paragraph chosen. (2) Distractor Selection Task: Workers validated previously generated question-answer pairs and selected up to two of six model-suggested distractors and wrote at least one distractor themselves to create a total of three distractors. Workers could mark questions as ungrammatical, having false answers, being unrelated to science or requiring very specific background knowledge. The proportion of questions passing validation was 92.8%.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the distractor selection task, crowd workers found the predicted distractors good enough to include in the final question around half of the time, resulting in 36.1% of the distractors in the final dataset being generated by the model. Acceptance rates were higher for short answers, with almost none accepted for very long answers. A qualitative evaluation showed that humans could not distinguish crowdsourced questions from original exam questions at a statistically significant level (55% identification rate, below p=0.05 significance).
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three answer distractors per question, with workers required to write at least one distractor themselves and allowed to select up to two from six model-suggested distractors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with Master's status. A total of 175 workers participated in the whole crowdsourcing project.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A distractor ranking model using a random forest classifier trained on 3705 science exam questions (4th and 8th grade) to predict plausible answer distractors. The model used features including GloVe embeddings, POS-tag consistency, string edit distance, WordNet-based hypernymy indicators, and knowledge-base links from OpenIE triples extracted from Simple Wikipedia.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Neural models did not outperform simple information retrieval baselines on the multiple choice version of the dataset, even when using the same background information. The dataset is useful for studying reading comprehension models in medium-data settings where training examples number in the tens of thousands instead of hundreds of thousands.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset has two versions: (1) Multiple choice version for selecting the correct answer given a question and several answer options using background information, and (2) Direct answer version where given a passage and question, systems must predict the span within the passage that answers the question. The dataset can be used as additional training data to improve performance on real science exams, with experiments showing accuracy improvements on 4th and 8th grade science exam questions when SciQ was added to training data.
